title: Frontend fundamentals and a usable web interface
intro: An interface translates a person's intent into operations they can understand. Today you will learn the different responsibilities of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, connect a form to a calculation, and build a small expense dashboard. A framework can help later, but it should not hide the browser concepts you need to inspect and debug.
objectives: Explain how HTML structure, CSS presentation, and JavaScript behavior cooperate.
Handle a form submission with validation and visible feedback.
Test an interface with keyboard input, a narrow screen, and a new user.

concepts.title: Structure communicates meaning
concepts.text: HTML describes the document and its controls. A heading introduces a section; a label identifies an input; a button performs an action. Use those elements instead of treating every part of the interface as a clickable box. The browser and assistive technology can then expose useful behavior and names. A placeholder is a temporary hint, not a reliable replacement for a visible label. Start with a semantic interface that works before adding decorative styling.

concepts.title: Presentation should support the task
concepts.text: CSS controls layout, spacing, typography, and visual states. A readable interface has a clear order, adequate contrast, and enough room for its controls. Test a narrow viewport rather than assuming a desktop layout shrinks automatically. Avoid conveying an error only through colour: provide a message. Focus indicators help keyboard users see which control will receive the next action. Small, consistent styling decisions are usually more useful than several unrelated visual effects.

concepts.title: Behavior connects events to state
concepts.text: JavaScript handles events such as submitting a form. The handler reads input, validates it, updates state, and renders feedback. Python and JavaScript use different syntax, but the input → process → output pattern remains. Browser validation improves usability, yet a future backend must validate its own inputs because browser controls can be bypassed. A localStorage demo persists data in one browser; it is not a shared server database or an authenticated account.

example.run: Open index.html in a browser or paste it into the HTML/CSS lab. Try the form with a keyboard as well as a pointer.
example.context: A labelled form updates a total in integer cents. The JavaScript checks the value again before changing state.
example.code:
Expense dashboard

Total: 0 cents
example.output:
The initial screen shows Total: 0 cents.
Submitting 250 shows Total: 250 cents.
Submitting another 100 shows Total: 350 cents.
example.walkthrough: The label and input are connected by matching for and id values. The submit handler prevents a normal page navigation, reads the input as text, and converts it deliberately. Validation occurs before changing total. textContent displays a text value without interpreting it as HTML. The status region provides feedback. This starter has only an accumulated in-memory total; your project will add named records, an empty state, persistence, and useful recovery.

exercises.title: Trace an event
exercises.task: Explain what happens between pressing the button and seeing the new total.
exercises.hint: Name the event, input boundary, validation, state change, and render step.
exercises.check: You can predict the result for two consecutive submissions.

exercises.title: Use a keyboard
exercises.task: Complete the form using Tab and Enter, then inspect the focus indicator.
exercises.hint: Native controls provide much of the basic keyboard behavior.
exercises.check: The task is possible without a mouse and the input has a useful name.

exercises.title: Test a small screen
exercises.task: Inspect the page at a 375px viewport and with longer labels or expense names.
exercises.hint: Look for clipped controls and page-wide horizontal scrolling.
exercises.check: The primary task remains readable and usable.

mistakes: Using placeholder text as the only input label.
Treating client-side validation as a future backend security boundary.
Confusing a one-browser localStorage record with a shared customer database.
fde: A customer experiences the workflow, not the internal class names. An FDE watches whether intended users can complete the task, understand feedback, and recover from mistakes. Accessibility and error states are part of that task, not optional polish added after the demo.

project.title: Responsive expense dashboard
project.brief: A freelancer wants to add labelled expenses, see a list and total, remove a mistaken record, and return to the data later in the same browser. Build a semantic HTML/CSS/JavaScript interface using fictional data. Document that browser-local persistence is a learning constraint and does not provide shared accounts or server-side authorization.
deliverables: A responsive form, expense list, total, and empty state.
Clear labels, keyboard behavior, and validation messages.
Browser-local persistence with useful handling of damaged saved data.
A usability and narrow-viewport test report.

milestones.title: Build the task structure
steps: Sketch the add, inspect, and remove workflow with semantic controls.
Add labels and readable empty-state feedback before styling.
milestones.check: A user can identify the primary action without explanation.

milestones.title: Connect state and behavior
steps: Store individual expense records and derive the total from them.
Validate submissions and restore saved records carefully.
milestones.check: A rejected record does not enter the list or total.

milestones.title: Verify the experience
steps: Test keyboard interaction, reload, and a 375px viewport.
Observe a new user and improve one concrete hesitation.
milestones.check: The main task remains usable across the tested conditions.

acceptance: Adding and removing named expenses updates the list and total correctly.
Form controls have visible labels and work with a keyboard.
Invalid input has a useful message and does not change stored data.
Data survives a reload in the same browser with documented limits.
The task works at 375px without page-wide horizontal overflow.
tests: Rejected according to the integer-cents contract
Saved data restored and controls remain usable
extensions: Add a category filter with a clearly labelled filtered total.
Move the calculation behind a validated API after lesson 24.
review: Which responsibilities belong to HTML, CSS, and JavaScript?
What behavior does your local persistence guarantee?
What changed after watching another person use the interface?

title: Deployment, configuration, and your first public application
intro: Deployment places a reproducible version of your application where its intended users can access it. That changes the environment, not just the URL. Today you will publish your expense dashboard, verify the actual hosted result, and document how to recover from an incorrect release.
objectives: Distinguish development source, a deployable artifact, and a running hosted version.
Verify assets, routes, and core behavior on the real deployment.
Document release identity, configuration ownership, and recovery.

concepts.title: An artifact is the version you deploy
concepts.text: A static site can consist of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and data assets. A framework may transform source files into a build directory before hosting. Keep track of which commit produced the artifact, because an edited working file is not automatically the version served to users. Paths also matter: an asset reference that works at a root URL may fail under a repository subpath. Inspect the deployed network requests instead of assuming a successful upload proves the page is usable.

concepts.title: Hosted users have different conditions
concepts.text: A new user's browser does not contain your local storage, cached files, or development configuration. Test logged out or in a clean browser context, with a direct route and a reload. A localhost URL refers to the user's own device, not your development computer. A static frontend's code and configuration are visible to its visitors, so a future model API credential must stay on a trusted backend rather than being embedded in browser JavaScript.

concepts.title: A release needs an operating story
concepts.text: Document how the site is built, how a release is identified, and which checks establish successful startup. A simple rollback might redeploy a previous artifact, but stateful systems also require data compatibility considerations. Keep the recovery steps practical for the person who will operate the system. A public URL alone does not verify permissions, invalid input, or every route. Record the checks you actually performed and the limitations that remain.

example.run: Use this as a release record in your own project. Start a local static preview with python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 from the directory containing index.html; a local preview is not a public deployment.
example.context: A release record connects the source version to a real URL and observed behavior rather than a screenshot alone.
example.code:
# Release record
Source commit: fill in the actual commit ID
Artifact: directory containing index.html and its assets
Public URL: fill in the verified hosted URL
Checks:
- Clean browser can open the home page
- Form validation and add/remove workflow work
- Asset requests succeed
- Narrow viewport remains usable
- Reload preserves only the documented browser-local data
Recovery: redeploy the previously verified artifact
Known limits: browser-local data; no shared accounts
example.output:
A completed release record contains an actual commit, hosted URL, observed check results, and a practical recovery step.
Placeholders are not evidence of a deployed application.
example.walkthrough: The commit identifies the reviewed source. The artifact identifies what the host receives. The public URL must be checked after deployment, not invented from an expected naming pattern. Each check should contain a result and relevant evidence. Recovery points to a previously verified version. This record prevents you from confusing local success with hosted success and makes a handoff understandable to someone who did not perform the deployment.

exercises.title: Inspect an asset path
exercises.task: Compare a relative asset URL with a root-relative URL under a repository subpath.
exercises.hint: A leading slash refers to the origin root, not automatically the application's folder.
exercises.check: You can explain why one path can work locally and fail after hosting.

exercises.title: Test as a new user
exercises.task: Open the hosted dashboard in a clean browser and complete its core task.
exercises.hint: Do not depend on your existing saved demo records.
exercises.check: The first-use and empty states are understandable.

exercises.title: Write a recovery sequence
exercises.task: Describe how to return to a known good static artifact and how to verify it.
exercises.hint: Name the version and the checks, not merely a generic undo instruction.
exercises.check: Another person could follow the steps without guessing which release to use.

mistakes: Sharing localhost as if it were a public application URL.
Embedding API secrets in a static frontend's source or build settings.
Assuming upload success verifies routes, assets, and user behavior.
fde: An FDE owns delivery beyond a local demonstration. Release identity, hosted checks, configuration responsibility, and recovery connect the implementation to the customer's operational reality. Even a small static dashboard should have a clear handoff.

project.title: A verified public expense dashboard
project.brief: Publish the dashboard from lesson 13 in your own learner project repository or chosen static host. Verify the deployed site in a clean browser, test a narrow viewport and reload, and record the release identity. Keep setup and recovery instructions alongside the project. Do not change the academy's hosting configuration as part of your learner exercise.
deliverables: A verified public URL and the source commit that produced it.
Build or publishing instructions for the chosen host.
A completed hosted verification checklist.
A release note, known limits, and recovery steps.

milestones.title: Prepare the artifact
steps: Inspect the files the host should serve and the asset path assumptions.
Publish from your own project with documented configuration.
milestones.check: The artifact corresponds to a specific reviewed source version.

milestones.title: Verify the real URL
steps: Open the actual hosted result in a clean context.
Exercise the form, remove action, reload, and small viewport.
milestones.check: The visible workflow and required assets work outside your development session.

milestones.title: Record operations
steps: Write release identity, observed checks, and limits.
Explain how a previous known good artifact could be restored.
milestones.check: The delivery record is useful to a future operator.

acceptance: A public URL serves the intended application version.
Required assets load under the actual hosting path.
Core form and expense workflows pass in a clean browser.
Direct loading, reload, and a narrow viewport are checked.
Release identity and recovery instructions are recorded.
tests: Open the verified public URL in a clean context
Load under the project's hosting subpath
Inspect a previous release and recovery instructions
A specific known good version and verification steps are identified
extensions: Automate build and publish checks for future changes.
Add a simple release-health check without collecting private user data.
review: What differed from your local environment?
What information would an operator need if the latest release failed?

title: Language models, tokens, context, and cost
intro: Language models can produce useful text and code, but fluent output is not evidence that an answer is correct. Today you will build an operational understanding of generation, token budgets, context limits, and cost. Your project is an experiment log that separates observed provider results from offline fixture demonstrations and estimates.
objectives: Explain why tokenization and fluent generation do not guarantee factual correctness.
Describe context and output budgets without assuming every model supports the same settings.
Calculate an estimate from explicit input/output usage and price assumptions.

concepts.title: Tokens are representation units
concepts.text: A tokenizer maps text into units used by the model. A token is not always a word: it can represent part of a word, punctuation, or another pattern depending on the tokenizer. Word counting is therefore not an exact token counter. A language model generates a continuation based on learned patterns and the supplied context; modern model systems can also use tools and additional processing. The practical lesson is that a convincing answer can still be unsupported, incomplete, or wrong.

concepts.title: Context is supplied, not unlimited memory
concepts.text: A model request contains some combination of instructions, conversation, retrieved content, and tool results. The service has limits and conventions for what fits and how output is budgeted. Applications may truncate or summarise conversation history rather than sending every previous message. Do not assume the model automatically knows a customer database or permanently remembers a prior session. Inspect the actual request you construct and the provider's documented limits for the chosen model.

concepts.title: Costs and controls are model-specific
concepts.text: An estimate should state request volume, input usage, output usage, and the relevant prices. Providers may distinguish cached, reasoning, image, tool, or other usage, so a simple text estimate is not a universal billing formula. Settings such as temperature are not supported identically by every model and do not turn generation into a factual verification process. Record the model and version, supported settings, observed usage, and the difference between an assumption and a measured result.

example.run: Run python model_budget.py. The prices and usage below are fictional exercise assumptions, not current provider quotes.
example.context: Input and output have separate assumed prices. The example is a transparent budget estimate, not a model call.
example.code:
requests = 2000
input_tokens_per_request = 1000
output_tokens_per_request = 500
input_price_per_million = 1.0
output_price_per_million = 4.0
input_cost = requests * input_tokens_per_request / 1_000_000 * input_price_per_million
output_cost = requests * output_tokens_per_request / 1_000_000 * output_price_per_million
print(f"Fictional estimate: ${input_cost + output_cost:.2f}")
print("Includes text input/output only; verify provider usage and prices separately")
example.output:
Fictional estimate: $6.00
Includes text input/output only; verify provider usage and prices separately
example.walkthrough: The two usage quantities are multiplied by the expected request count and converted to millions to match the assumed price units. Separating input and output exposes which assumption drives the estimate. Doubling output length raises output cost independently of input cost. The final line states the estimate's scope. For a real provider experiment, use documented usage fields and current prices instead of treating this sample as a quote or a universal formula.

exercises.title: Inspect representation
exercises.task: Compare the word count of a sentence with a supported tokenizer's output when one is available.
exercises.hint: Label a word-based approximation as approximate rather than exact tokens.
exercises.check: Your note distinguishes text words from model-specific token units.

exercises.title: Change budget assumptions
exercises.task: Double request count, then double output length, explaining which costs change.
exercises.hint: Keep assumptions in named variables rather than editing a final dollar figure.
exercises.check: Each result follows from the stated formula and scope.

exercises.title: Plan a model experiment
exercises.task: Define three prompts, a scoring rule, supported settings, and an output limit before making optional provider calls.
exercises.hint: Use an offline response fixture if no provider access is available, and label it clearly.
exercises.check: Fixture results are not reported as observed model performance.

mistakes: Calling tokens words or a unit of thought rather than a model representation.
Assuming every turn contains the entire history or every model supports identical settings.
Publishing fictional prices or mocked outputs as measured provider facts.
fde: A customer needs a useful, affordable, assessable service. An FDE can explain what information the model receives, what it does not know, what a request is likely to cost under stated assumptions, and how output quality will be checked.

project.title: LLM experiment and budget notebook
project.brief: A team is deciding whether a model could help with short support summaries. Create a small experiment record containing prompts, response examples, scoring criteria, latency/usage fields, and a cost estimate. Support an offline fixture mode for learning and an optional real-provider mode. Never combine the two modes into an unlabeled performance claim.
deliverables: An experiment log with model or fixture identity and request settings.
Three prompt cases with a human-readable quality rubric.
A usage/cost calculator with explicit scope and assumptions.
A comparison note distinguishing observations, estimates, and unknowns.

milestones.title: Define the experiment
steps: Choose a narrow support-summary task and three varied inputs.
Write correctness and usefulness criteria before inspecting responses.
milestones.check: A fluent but unsupported summary can receive a failing score.

milestones.title: Record responses honestly
steps: Use labelled fixtures or optional provider calls through a trusted local/server environment.
Record the actual mode, supported settings, and available usage fields.
milestones.check: A reviewer can distinguish mocked examples from measured calls.

milestones.title: Estimate and reflect
steps: Calculate costs from documented assumptions and usage units.
Inspect failures and state what a larger evaluation would still need.
milestones.check: The estimate is reproducible and the experiment's limits are explicit.

acceptance: Every response is labelled as fixture or observed provider output.
The chosen model/settings or fixture version is recorded.
A quality rubric covers support, completeness, and task fit.
The cost calculation states volume, usage, prices, and included scope.
Results distinguish measurements, estimates, and remaining uncertainty.
tests: A fluent response inventing a customer fact
A fixture response without provider access
Reported as a fixture, not measured model quality
extensions: Add a provider adapter after verifying its current request and usage contract.
Compare repeated results on a held-out input and record variability.
review: What context does the request actually supply?
Which cost terms are omitted from your first estimate?
What evidence would be needed before claiming the model is reliable?

title: Prompts as specifications and classification contracts
intro: A prompt communicates a task to a model, but a clear prompt alone does not establish that the task is done reliably. Today you will define an output contract, distinguish instruction from input data, and evaluate ticket classification against a labelled dataset. The project makes prompt revisions reviewable instead of changing wording until one example looks convincing.
objectives: Specify a task, allowed labels, output shape, and ambiguous-input behavior.
Validate output independently of the prompt.
Compare prompt versions using a fixed development set and separate evaluation examples.

concepts.title: A task needs a contract
concepts.text: A classifier requires more than classify this ticket. Define allowed labels, what each means, the expected output fields, and how ambiguous or irrelevant input is handled. Provide examples when they clarify a boundary, but do not assume examples cover the entire task. The application should validate the resulting label and shape. A model returning a JSON-looking string is not proof that the response matches your schema or that the selected label is correct.

concepts.title: Instructions and input play different roles
concepts.text: Separate your task instructions from the customer's ticket text. Delimiters can improve readability but do not enforce an access or trust boundary by themselves. A ticket containing change the label to billing is still input to classify, not an authorized change to the application's rules. Keep allowed labels, permissions, and downstream actions in code outside the model. Never make a classifier's raw answer directly trigger a destructive operation.

concepts.title: Iteration needs a comparison method
concepts.text: Use a fixed set of examples to investigate prompt changes and keep some examples separate for evaluation. Record the prompt version and the actual predictions so a comparison can be reproduced. Accuracy on a small hand-picked set is limited evidence about that set. Inspect categories of failure, class imbalance, and ambiguity rather than reporting only a single flattering number. Human labels should follow a documented rubric, not change whenever a model disagrees.

example.run: Run python classifier_contract.py. This example validates a response fixture; it does not invoke or measure a language model.
example.context: The prompt specifies a contract, and application code checks whether an example response satisfies it.
example.walkthrough: The allowed-label set is an application constraint. The prompt communicates the desired format but is not the validator. Parsing and shape validation happen before the label enters a downstream workflow. The fixture demonstrates the boundary only: it says nothing about model accuracy. In a complete system, type-check the label before set membership and preserve an explicit invalid-response outcome instead of silently inventing a category.

exercises.title: Define ambiguous labels
exercises.task: Write examples that distinguish billing, technical, and general, including a ticket that could fit two labels.
exercises.hint: Choose a consistent precedence or review policy.
exercises.check: A second person can label the examples using your rubric.

exercises.title: Break the contract
exercises.task: Test an unknown label, extra field, malformed JSON, and a non-string label.
exercises.hint: Validation must handle types before operations that assume those types.
exercises.check: Invalid output has a visible failure category.

exercises.title: Compare two versions
exercises.task: Change one prompt requirement and record predictions on the same examples.
exercises.hint: Keep evaluation examples separate from examples used to tune the wording.
exercises.check: Your report can show both improvements and regressions.

mistakes: Treating a well-written prompt as a replacement for output validation.
Using the tuning examples as the only evidence of general quality.
Calling deterministic fixture validation measured language-model accuracy.
fde: Customers need stable behavior and explainable exceptions. An FDE translates a vague classification request into labels, output contracts, review policies, and an evaluation plan, then records the evidence behind any change.

project.title: Versioned support-ticket classifier
project.brief: A support team wants to route tickets into billing, technical, and general queues. Build a labelled dataset, a versioned prompt, an output validator, and a comparison report. Fixture mode lets you verify the pipeline without provider access; optional real-provider mode lets you collect predictions. Ambiguous and invalid outputs must not silently trigger routing.
deliverables: A label rubric and at least 12 labelled ticket examples.
Versioned prompts with one clearly explained revision.
A parser/validator and an explicit review or rejection result.
A comparison report separating fixture checks from real predictions.

milestones.title: Specify and label
steps: Define category meanings and ambiguous-input behavior.
Create varied cases and reserve some from prompt tuning.
milestones.check: The target labels are justified by the rubric rather than the model.

milestones.title: Build the response boundary
steps: Validate JSON shape, label type, and allowed values.
Keep invalid results out of automatic downstream routing.
milestones.check: Malformed output cannot become a successful routing result.

milestones.title: Evaluate a revision
steps: Record prompt versions and predictions on a consistent set.
Inspect false classifications and report held-out results separately.
milestones.check: The comparison includes regressions and uncertainty, not only successes.

acceptance: Allowed categories and ambiguity policy are documented.
At least 12 labelled examples include boundary and invalid-input cases.
Response parsing validates shape, types, and allowed labels.
Prompt versions and predictions are recorded for comparison.
Fixture checks and real-provider evaluations are reported separately.
tests: Unknown label, extra fields, or invalid JSON
Ticket text instructing the system to change its rules
Treated as input data, not an authorized rule change
extensions: Add a human-review queue for uncertain or invalid outputs.
Report per-category errors and class balance instead of accuracy alone.
review: Which constraints are enforced by code rather than the prompt?
How do development cases differ from held-out evaluation cases?
What would make an apparent score improvement misleading?

title: Structured outputs, validated tools, and safe execution boundaries
intro: Tool use connects a model's proposed action to code that can perform it. The crucial engineering boundary is the application's decision to accept, reject, or require review of that proposal. Today you will build a small allowlisted dispatcher and learn why a tool schema, validation, authorization, and actual execution are separate concerns.
objectives: Describe the loop from model proposal to tool result and final response.
Validate tool names and argument types before execution.
Keep authorization and consequential actions outside model control.

concepts.title: A proposal is not an authorized action
concepts.text: A model may return a tool name and arguments. Your program decides whether the name exists, the arguments are valid, and the user is allowed to perform the action. A schema helps communicate the contract but does not replace application checks. Never pass arbitrary model-proposed text into eval, a shell, or unrestricted SQL. Use a small dispatcher that maps recognized names to specific functions and handles unsupported proposals visibly.

concepts.title: Validate before calling
concepts.text: Check outer shape, required fields, types, ranges, and unexpected fields before passing values to a tool. An integer-looking string is not automatically an integer argument. Decide whether additional fields are rejected or ignored, and keep the policy consistent. Authorization depends on trusted identity and resource policy, not a role field supplied inside model arguments. A successful tool call returns structured data that the application can inspect before it is presented to the user.

concepts.title: Side effects add operational requirements
concepts.text: A read-only lookup has a different impact from sending an email or charging a card. For consequential actions, define approval, idempotency, logging, and recovery responsibilities. A repeated request should not accidentally repeat a financial or external action. Tool timeouts and errors must have explicit results rather than being transformed into invented success messages. Begin with a read-only tool while learning the contract and observation loop.

example.run: Run python tool_dispatcher.py. The call is a fixture proposal and the tool reads fictional local inventory.
example.context: Only one tool exists. Its contract accepts exactly one non-blank product ID.
example.walkthrough: The dispatcher checks the recognized operation before considering arguments. It verifies the argument shape and product-ID type before lookup. The data is a fictional read-only inventory, so the example has no payment or messaging side effect. A complete dispatcher should first validate that the proposal itself is a dictionary, enforce resource access using trusted identity, and record a safe tool result. This fixture validates the application boundary, not a model's ability to choose tools.

exercises.title: Draw the action loop
exercises.task: Show the user request, model proposal, application checks, tool result, and final response as separate steps.
exercises.check: You can identify which component can reject a proposal.

exercises.title: Reject unsupported proposals
exercises.task: Test an unknown tool, an array as arguments, an extra field, and an empty product ID.
exercises.hint: Validate structure before operations that assume a dictionary or string.
exercises.check: None of the invalid proposals executes a different tool.

exercises.title: Discuss a side-effect tool
exercises.task: Write the additional controls required before a hypothetical send-email tool could be used.
exercises.hint: Include permission, approval, repeated requests, and failure reporting.
exercises.check: A model cannot authorize itself by supplying a role or approval argument.

mistakes: Executing a tool proposal merely because the model emitted it.
Using eval or unrestricted command strings as a tool implementation.
Checking argument shape but omitting trusted user and resource authorization.
fde: The most valuable customer integrations often touch existing records and workflows. An FDE defines the exact allowed operations and their trust boundaries, so natural-language convenience does not silently widen the customer's permissions.

project.title: An allowlisted inventory tool service
project.brief: A shop assistant needs read-only stock lookup and product search over fictional inventory. Build a dispatcher with two named tools, argument validation, not-found results, and a trusted-user access policy. Demonstrate invalid proposals and resource restrictions with fixtures before optionally connecting a model that proposes tool calls.
deliverables: Two documented read-only tool contracts and a dispatcher.
A fictional inventory dataset and trusted-user policy fixtures.
Tests for invalid names, arguments, and forbidden resources.
A trace of proposal, validation, execution, and tool result.

milestones.title: Define narrow operations
steps: Specify lookup and search inputs, results, and not-found behavior.
List explicitly excluded write operations.
milestones.check: The contract cannot place orders or change stock.

milestones.title: Enforce the boundary
steps: Validate proposals and dispatch only recognized operations.
Apply trusted access policy before reading a resource.
milestones.check: Model-supplied arguments cannot grant extra access.

milestones.title: Inspect execution
steps: Record safe tool traces and simulate invalid or timed-out calls.
Keep failures distinguishable from successful results.
milestones.check: A reviewer can see why each call was accepted or rejected.

acceptance: Only the two documented read-only tools can execute.
Names, shapes, types, and ranges are validated before calls.
Trusted user/resource policy is enforced outside model arguments.
Not-found, forbidden, and failed-call results remain distinguishable.
A safe execution trace and invalid-proposal tests are recorded.
tests: Valid stock lookup for an allowed product
Unknown tool or unexpected argument field
Model arguments claim an admin role
Ignored as authority; trusted policy still applies
Not-found or forbidden result without fabricated stock
extensions: Add a model adapter while keeping the same validated dispatcher.
Design a write tool on paper with approval and idempotency; do not silently add it to the read-only pilot.
review: Who decides whether the tool is authorized?
What changes when a tool has external side effects?
Which trace fields are useful without exposing private content?

title: Embeddings, vector similarity, and retrieval evaluation
intro: Embeddings represent information as vectors that can support similarity search. A similarity score is not a fact check, and a plausible example is not proof that retrieval will work on a customer's data. Today you will inspect the mathematics with small illustrative vectors, then design a FAQ-search project with labelled queries and a clear comparison method.
objectives: Explain vectors, dimensions, and cosine similarity in practical terms.
Distinguish illustrative vectors from learned embedding-model output.
Evaluate keyword and vector retrieval using expected relevant documents.

concepts.title: An embedding model supplies a representation
concepts.text: A learned embedding model maps input into a vector space. The vector's usefulness depends on the model, training, and task. Similarity in that space can help find related content, but it does not guarantee that a document answers the question or is true. Do not combine document and query vectors produced by incompatible models or dimensions. Record which model and configuration created an index so future queries use a compatible representation.

concepts.title: Cosine compares direction
concepts.text: For non-zero vectors of equal dimension, cosine similarity divides their dot product by the product of their lengths. This helps compare direction rather than raw magnitude. A zero vector needs an explicit policy because its cosine denominator is zero. A mismatched dimension is invalid input, not a reason to silently ignore extra coordinates. Small hand-authored vectors make the formula understandable, but their chosen directions are not evidence that a real model captured semantic meaning.

concepts.title: Retrieval needs labelled queries
concepts.text: Define which documents should be relevant to a query before judging the ranking. Inspect top-k results, exact-identifier queries, paraphrases, and questions with no useful match. Keyword search can be effective for product codes and exact terms; vector retrieval can help with some semantic variations. Compare them on your actual task rather than assuming one always wins. A threshold tuned on one example can fail elsewhere, so include varied and held-out queries.

example.run: Run python vector_search.py. These vectors are hand-authored mathematical illustrations, not learned semantic embeddings.
example.context: The example validates dimensions and non-zero lengths before calculating a score.
example.walkthrough: The function first enforces the mathematical input contract. Each norm is the square root of the sum of squared coordinates. zip pairs compatible coordinates for the dot product. The division produces a direction-based similarity for the supplied vectors. The final result describes this mathematical example only. To investigate real semantic retrieval, replace the illustrative vectors with a documented model's outputs and evaluate relevant-document ranking on independent query labels.

exercises.title: Compare directions
exercises.task: Compute similarity for identical, perpendicular, and opposite illustrative vectors.
exercises.check: The scores are 1, 0, and -1 within numerical tolerance.

exercises.title: Validate the contract
exercises.task: Test mismatched dimensions and a zero vector.
exercises.hint: Reject before dividing or silently truncating with zip.
exercises.check: Both failures produce a clear error.

exercises.title: Define relevance
exercises.task: Write six FAQ queries with expected relevant document IDs, including an exact code and a no-answer query.
exercises.hint: Label the expected evidence before looking at ranked output.
exercises.check: You can explain why each document does or does not answer its query.

mistakes: Treating similarity as proof that a source is correct or relevant enough to answer.
Mixing vectors from incompatible models or ignoring dimension mismatches.
Presenting hand-authored vectors as measured model performance.
fde: A customer's search problem is about finding useful information under actual data and access constraints. An FDE measures retrieval on representative queries, records index identity, and explains where keyword, vector, or hybrid search fits the task.

project.title: FAQ retrieval comparison workbench
project.brief: A team wants staff to find the right FAQ despite variations in wording. Build a small FAQ dataset, a keyword baseline, a vector-search implementation, and labelled query results. Begin with clearly labelled illustrative vectors if needed; optionally add a real embedding model. Compare the methods honestly and preserve a no-match outcome.
deliverables: At least 10 FAQ records with stable IDs and source text.
Keyword and vector ranking functions with clear input contracts.
At least six queries with expected relevant IDs.
A comparison report naming the representation and its limits.

milestones.title: Prepare evidence
steps: Write the FAQ records and label representative query relevance.
Include exact identifiers, paraphrases, and missing-answer cases.
milestones.check: Relevance labels exist before ranking results are inspected.

milestones.title: Implement comparable retrieval
steps: Build the keyword baseline and validated vector similarity.
Record whether vectors are illustrative or from a specified model.
milestones.check: Both methods return ranked document IDs that can be inspected.

milestones.title: Evaluate and explain
steps: Compare useful hits and failure cases on the same queries.
Document an explicit no-match policy and a potential improvement.
milestones.check: The report does not claim learned semantic performance from hand-authored vectors.

acceptance: FAQ records and query relevance use stable IDs.
Keyword and vector methods are evaluated on the same labelled queries.
Vector dimensions and zero-length inputs are validated.
The vector model or illustrative-fixture identity is recorded.
No-answer queries and observed retrieval failures are reported.
tests: Identical, perpendicular, and opposite example vectors
Baseline comparison records whether the relevant FAQ is retrieved
Question not answered by any FAQ
No useful match rather than forced success
extensions: Use a documented embedding model and rerun the independent relevance cases.
Compare a hybrid method while recording what changed and why.
review: What does a cosine score establish and what does it not establish?
Why must index and query representations be compatible?
Which query shows a meaningful difference between your retrieval methods?
